questions.question: What is a thread in Java and how does it differ from a process?
questions.title: Thread vs Process in Java
questions.direct_answer: A **process** is an independent program in execution with its own memory space. A **thread** is the smallest unit of execution within a process — threads share the process's **heap memory** but each has its own **stack**. Multiple threads in one process can run concurrently and share data.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying threads are completely isolated — they share heap memory, which is both their power and risk
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain shared heap as the reason for race conditions, and the context switch cost difference

sections.title: Thread vs Process
sections.content:
| Aspect | Process | Thread |
|---|---|---|
| Memory | Own address space | Shared heap, own stack |
| Creation cost | Heavy — OS allocates memory | Light — within existing process |
| Communication | Inter-process (sockets, pipes) | Shared memory (direct) |
| Failure isolation | Crash doesn't affect others | Crash can kill the whole process |
| Context switch | Expensive | Cheaper |
| Example | JVM itself is a process | Each request handler thread |

sections.title: What Threads Share
sections.content:
Within a Java process (JVM), threads share:
- **Heap memory** — all objects created with `new` live here
- **Class metadata** (method area)
- **Open file descriptors**

Each thread has its own:
- **Stack** — method call frames, local variables
- **Program counter** — which instruction is executing
- **Thread-local storage** (if used)

The shared heap is why threads can communicate easily — but also why **race conditions** happen.

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: A process is an independent program with its own memory space — like the JVM itself is a process. A thread is a unit of execution within that process. The key difference is memory: processes are isolated from each other, but threads within the same process share the heap. That shared heap is what makes threads powerful — they can communicate through shared objects without the overhead of inter-process communication. But it's also what makes threads risky — two threads accessing and modifying the same object simultaneously can corrupt data. That's the root cause of race conditions.

groups.heading: Process
groups.text: A process is an independent running program with its own memory space. When you start the JVM, it's a process. It can't directly read another process's memory.

groups.heading: Thread
groups.text: A thread is the smallest unit of execution inside a process. All threads in one JVM share the heap but each has its own stack. That's what lets them coordinate — and what causes race conditions.

items: Use threads when tasks need to share data quickly — like multiple order-handler threads sharing an order queue.
Use separate processes when isolation matters — like separate microservices where one crashing shouldn't kill others.

speakable_v2.cap: Threads are powerful because they share memory, and risky for exactly the same reason.

questions.question: What is the main thread in a Java application?
questions.title: Main Thread in Java Applications
questions.direct_answer: The **main thread** is the first thread created by the JVM when a Java program starts. It executes the `public static void main(String[] args)` method. All other threads are typically spawned from the main thread. When the main thread finishes, the JVM exits if no other non-daemon threads are running.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic thread awareness — understanding how Java programs start
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking the JVM exits as soon as main() returns — it waits for all non-daemon threads
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention daemon threads and how they differ from non-daemon threads

sections.title: The Main Thread
sections.content:
When you run a Java program, the JVM:
1. Creates the main thread
2. Main thread calls `main(String[] args)`
3. Main thread can create additional threads
4. JVM waits until all **non-daemon** threads finish before exiting

**Non-daemon threads** (user threads) keep the JVM alive. **Daemon threads** are background threads that are killed automatically when all non-daemon threads finish (e.g., garbage collector thread).

You can access the main thread programmatically via `Thread.currentThread()` inside main().

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Main thread has the highest priority by default (5)
- Thread.currentThread() returns a reference to the current running thread
- JVM exits when all non-daemon threads complete, even if main() returned
- If main() throws an uncaught exception, the main thread dies but other threads may continue
- Daemon threads: thread.setDaemon(true) — must be called before thread.start()

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: The main thread is the thread the JVM creates automatically to run the main() method. It's the entry point of every Java application. All other threads in your application are typically started from the main thread or from threads that the main thread started. One important thing: the JVM doesn't exit as soon as main() returns. It waits until all non-daemon threads are finished. So if your main thread starts a new thread and returns, the JVM keeps running until that new thread also completes. Daemon threads are the exception — they're background threads like the garbage collector that get killed automatically when all user threads finish.

questions.question: What is multithreading and why is it used in Java applications?
questions.title: Multithreading Benefits in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Multithreading** means running multiple threads concurrently within a single process. It's used to improve **performance** (utilizing multiple CPU cores), maintain **responsiveness** (UI doesn't freeze while background work runs), and handle **concurrent users** in server applications.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of why multithreading exists — not just what it is
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not giving concrete use cases — just saying 'to do things simultaneously'
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect to Spring Boot request handling — each HTTP request runs in its own thread

sections.title: When Multithreading Helps
sections.content:
- **Server applications**: Spring Boot handles each HTTP request in a separate thread from a thread pool — 200 concurrent users = 200 threads working simultaneously
- **CPU-bound tasks**: Parallelize computation across multiple CPU cores
- **I/O-bound tasks**: One thread does file I/O while others serve requests
- **Background jobs**: Email sending, report generation — don't block the user request thread
- **Responsiveness**: Desktop/Android apps keep UI thread unblocked

sections.title: Multithreading in Spring Boot Context
sections.content:
In a Spring Boot REST application, multithreading works by default:

- Embedded Tomcat maintains a **thread pool** (default 200 threads)
- Each incoming HTTP request gets **its own thread** from the pool
- While one user's request is waiting for a DB query, another user's request runs on a different thread
- Without multithreading, users would queue up and be served one at a time

This is why **thread safety** matters — if a Spring bean stores state in instance fields, 200 threads will race to read/write it.

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Multithreading is about running multiple threads at the same time within one process. The main reason to use it in Java server applications like Spring Boot is concurrency — handling multiple users simultaneously. Tomcat keeps a thread pool and gives each HTTP request its own thread. So if 100 users hit your API at the same time, 100 threads are working in parallel. Without that, users would queue up and get terrible response times. The other use case is not blocking on I/O — while one thread waits for a database response, other threads can keep processing. The downside is complexity: shared state needs to be managed carefully to avoid race conditions.

questions.question: What is a thread-safe class in Java?
questions.title: Thread-Safe Classes in Java
questions.direct_answer: A **thread-safe** class behaves correctly when accessed from multiple threads simultaneously without external synchronization. It prevents **data corruption** by ensuring that concurrent operations on its state are atomic or properly synchronized.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of thread safety as a design property — not just a technical term
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking all Java classes are thread-safe by default — ArrayList, HashMap are not
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give examples of thread-safe vs non-thread-safe classes and the mechanism that makes each safe

sections.title: Thread-Safe vs Not Thread-Safe
sections.content:
| Class | Thread-Safe? | Why |
|---|---|---|
| ArrayList | No | No synchronization on add/remove |
| Vector | Yes | All methods synchronized |
| HashMap | No | No synchronization |
| ConcurrentHashMap | Yes | Segment locking |
| StringBuilder | No | Not synchronized |
| StringBuffer | Yes | All methods synchronized |
| AtomicInteger | Yes | Compare-and-swap operations |

sections.title: Making Code Thread-Safe
sections.content:
A class becomes thread-safe through:
1. **Immutability** — String is thread-safe because it's immutable; no state changes
2. **Synchronization** — `synchronized` methods/blocks ensure one thread at a time
3. **Atomic operations** — `AtomicInteger`, `AtomicReference` use CPU-level CAS
4. **Thread-local storage** — each thread gets its own copy of the variable
5. **No shared state** — stateless classes (like most Spring controllers) are inherently thread-safe

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: A thread-safe class is one that works correctly when multiple threads use it simultaneously without you needing to add external synchronization. Not all Java classes are thread-safe — ArrayList and HashMap are not, for example. Thread safety can be achieved in several ways: making the class immutable like String, synchronizing all methods like Vector does, using atomic operations like AtomicInteger, or simply having no shared mutable state. The most elegant approach in a Spring application is stateless classes — if your controller or service doesn't store anything in instance fields, there's nothing to protect.

beats.text: A thread-safe class works correctly when multiple threads use it simultaneously without you adding any external synchronization. Its internal state stays consistent even when several threads call its methods at the same time.

In any multi-threaded app — like a Spring Boot order service with 200 request threads — shared data structures need to be safe. If they aren't, two threads can corrupt the structure's internals simultaneously.

items: Immutability: String is thread-safe because it can't be modified after creation.
Synchronization: Vector and StringBuffer synchronize every method.
Atomic operations: AtomicInteger uses CPU-level compare-and-swap — no blocking.
No shared state: stateless Spring beans have nothing to protect.

beats.text: non-obvious: ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe, but operations like get-then-put aren't atomic as a combined step. If two threads both check a key is absent and then both insert, you can still get unexpected results. Thread-safe class doesn't mean every multi-step operation on it is safe.

items: ArrayList and HashMap are not thread-safe — using them in multiple threads without synchronization causes corruption.
Stateless beans are the simplest form of thread safety — prefer them for Spring services.

speakable_v2.cap: Thread safety is a design property, not a language feature — you have to consciously choose how to achieve it.

questions.question: What is context switching in multithreading?
questions.title: Context Switching in Java Multithreading
questions.direct_answer: **Context switching** is when the CPU saves the state of the currently running thread and restores the state of a different thread to run next. It has overhead — saving/restoring registers, cache invalidation — which is why too many threads can hurt performance despite theoretical parallelism.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of threading costs — more threads isn't always better
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why thread pool size should be tuned and that more threads than cores causes more context switching

sections.title: Context Switching Overhead
sections.content:
When the OS scheduler switches from thread A to thread B:
1. Save thread A's registers, program counter, stack pointer
2. Restore thread B's saved state
3. Flush CPU caches (thread B might access different memory)
4. Thread B continues executing

This overhead is typically **microseconds** but adds up with hundreds of threads switching frequently.

Why this matters for Java:
- Creating thousands of threads (one per request) wastes time in context switching
- Thread **pools** control thread count — typically `CPU cores * 2` for CPU-bound, more for I/O-bound
- Context switch between threads in same process is cheaper than between processes

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Context switching is when the CPU stops running one thread and switches to another. To do this, it has to save everything about the current thread — registers, program counter, stack state — and restore the previously saved state of the next thread. This takes time and also causes CPU cache misses since the new thread accesses different memory. The practical implication is: creating thousands of threads doesn't give you thousands times the performance. At some point, you're spending more time context switching than doing actual work. That's why thread pools have a bounded size — typically tuned to the number of CPU cores plus some factor for I/O wait time.

beats.text: Context switching is when the CPU saves the complete state of the currently running thread — registers, program counter, stack pointer — and loads the saved state of a different thread so it can run next. This handoff has overhead.
CPUs have fewer cores than there are threads. The OS scheduler multiplexes many threads onto few cores by rapidly switching between them. Context switching is the cost of that sharing.

items: Register save/restore: all CPU registers for the outgoing thread are saved to memory.
Cache pressure: the incoming thread likely needs different memory, causing cache misses.
Scheduling overhead: the OS must decide which thread runs next.

beats.text: sharp edge: For your order app, Tomcat's default of 200 threads works because most threads spend time waiting on database I/O, not burning CPU. If you created 10,000 threads for CPU-heavy order processing, you'd spend more time context switching than processing — throughput would actually drop.

items: Creating one thread per task (instead of using a pool) at scale causes excessive context switching.
Thread pool size should be tuned: roughly CPU cores for CPU-bound, more for I/O-bound tasks.

speakable_v2.cap: Context switching is the hidden cost of concurrency — thread pools exist precisely to keep it under control.

questions.question: What is Thread.sleep() and does it release the lock?
questions.title: Thread.sleep() and Lock Release
questions.direct_answer: `Thread.sleep(milliseconds)` pauses the current thread for the specified time. Crucially, **sleep does NOT release any held locks** — if a thread sleeps while holding a `synchronized` lock, other threads waiting for that lock remain blocked.

interviewer_intent.testing: Classic gotcha — sleep vs wait distinction is a very common interview question
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking sleep releases the lock — it doesn't; wait() does
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Contrast with Object.wait() which does release the lock and must be in a synchronized block

sections.title: sleep() vs wait()
sections.content:
| Aspect | Thread.sleep() | Object.wait() |
|---|---|---|
| Class | Thread (static) | Object (instance) |
| Releases lock? | NO | YES |
| In synchronized block? | Not required | Required |
| Woken up by | Time expiry / interrupt | notify()/notifyAll() / interrupt |
| After waking | Continues | Must re-acquire lock |
| Use case | Pause for time | Wait for condition |

sections.title: How to Answer This in an Interview
sections.content: Thread.sleep() pauses the current thread for a given number of milliseconds. The critical thing to know is that sleep does NOT release any lock the thread is holding. So if Thread A is inside a synchronized block and calls sleep, other threads that need the same lock are still blocked — they can't get in even though Thread A is just waiting. This is different from Object.wait(), which does release the lock while waiting. That's the key distinction: sleep holds the lock, wait releases it. This is one of the most commonly asked multithreading questions in fresher interviews.

followup_questions: What is the difference between Thread.sleep() and Object.wait()?
What should you do when InterruptedException is thrown from sleep()?

groups.heading: Thread.sleep(ms)
groups.text: A static method on Thread. Pauses the current thread for the given milliseconds. It does NOT release any lock the thread holds. Other threads waiting for that lock stay blocked the entire time.

groups.heading: Object.wait()
groups.text: An instance method on Object. Must be inside a synchronized block. Releases the lock AND waits until notify() or notifyAll() is called. The thread re-acquires the lock before continuing.

items: Use sleep() when you just want to pause a thread for a fixed time — like a retry delay in a polling loop.
Use wait() when coordinating between threads around a shared condition — like a consumer waiting for items.

beats.text: If your order processor holds a synchronized lock and calls Thread.sleep(5000), every other order thread that needs that same lock is blocked for 5 full seconds — even though the processor is just waiting.

speakable_v2.cap: sleep() holds the lock and waits by time; wait() releases the lock and waits for a signal — they're for completely different situations.
